# Mahānidāna Sutta (DN 15 (PTS DN ii 55))

**ID:** DN 15 (PTS DN ii 55)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahānidāna Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Great Discourse on Causation
**PTS:** DN ii 55
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/dn15
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0102m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahānidāna Sutta* ("The Great Discourse on Causation", DN 15) is the fifteenth sutta of the *Dīghanikāya* and the longest, most comprehensive discourse on dependent arising (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) in the collection [Bodhi 1984; Bodhi 1995; SuttaCentral]. The narrative opens when Venerable Ānanda approaches the Buddha and remarks that the teaching of dependent origination appears simple and clear; the Buddha firmly rejects this assertion, warning that the doctrine is profound and deep, and proceeds to give a detailed exposition of conditional links [Bodhi 1984; SuttaCentral]. Notably, instead of the standard twelve-link sequence, the discourse presents a nine-link formulation that omits the first two links (ignorance and volitional formations) and sets forth a reciprocal conditioning relationship between consciousness (*viññāṇa*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) [Emmanuel 2013; Anālayo 2018; Meisig 2010]. The sutta also includes analyses of feeling (*vedanā*)—stressing that pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings do not coexist—and describes the seven stations of beings/consciousness in the context of rebirth and release [Jantrasrisalai 2008; Anālayo 2014; Anālayo 2018].

DN 15 has extensive textual connections across the Buddhist canons. Curated parallels include four Chinese translations—DĀ 13 (*Dīrgha-āgama*), MĀ 97 (*Madhyama-āgama*), T 14 (*Rén běn yù shēng jīng*), and T 52 (*Dà shēng yì jīng*)—as well as Sanskrit fragments (such as SHT sutta23, SF 138, and SF 240) and sections of the Sarvāstivāda *Dharmaskandha*, all aligned with high confidence by DharmaNexus [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Anālayo 2018; Meisig 2010]. In the Pali tradition, its opening is shared almost verbatim with SN 12:60, while large textual blocks are shared with the *Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅga* (Vb 6), *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33), and *Dasuttara Sutta* (DN 34) [Bodhi 2003; DharmaNexus]. The sutta also forms part of the traditional *Catubhāṇavārapāḷi* paritta collection [Anālayo 2018]. Its classical commentary in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and subcommentary were translated into English alongside the sutta by Bhikkhu Bodhi, with additional modern English translations produced by Thanissaro Bhikkhu and Bhikkhu Sujato [Bodhi 1984; Bodhi 1995; Emmanuel 2013; SuttaCentral].
